summary.text: Patient 1, a man aged 25 to 30, reported problematic alcohol use since his early teenage years with law, relationship and workplace problems, many unsuccessful attempts to stop, a rejected pharmacological treatment, ineffective prior psychotherapy and brief contact with Alcoholics Anonymous. He had alcohol use disorder and moderate major depressive disorder.

After a baseline period with a weekly mean of 3.3 binge drinking episodes (SD = 1.5), he received 12 one-hour sessions of metacognitive therapy and was followed up at 3 and 6 months. His weekly alcohol use fell substantially, with metacognitive beliefs decreasing gradually in the first half of treatment, and he was classified as recovered with no DSM-5 AUD criteria met at post-treatment and follow-up.

summary.text: Patient 2, a man aged 25 to 30, had alcohol use difficulties that began almost 10 years previously as a means of managing anxiety in social situations, relational problems because of behavior when drunk, and recurrent relapses after autonomous attempts to cut down. He had alcohol use disorder and social anxiety disorder, was medication free and had never had contact with mental health services.

After a baseline period with a weekly mean of 1.5 binge drinking episodes (SD = 0.6), he received 12 one-hour sessions of metacognitive therapy and was followed up at 3 and 6 months. His metacognitive beliefs decreased rapidly after treatment began, and he was classified as recovered with no DSM-5 AUD criteria met at post-treatment and follow-up.

summary.text: Patient 3, an unemployed man aged 35 to 40, could not continue his job because of drinking. His alcohol difficulties became serious 12 years earlier, he drank alone daily during the last 10 years with reduced social contacts, and he had alcohol use disorder and major depressive disorder.

After a baseline period with a weekly mean of 2.4 binge drinking episodes (SD = 0.5), he received 12 one-hour sessions of metacognitive therapy and was followed up at 3 and 6 months. His metacognitive beliefs decreased constantly across treatment. His QFS was below cut-off at post-treatment and 3 months, but at 6 months his weekly alcohol use (QFS = 20) and craving increased while staying below baseline; he met one DSM-5 AUD criterion and was classified as improved.

summary.text: Patient 4, a man aged 60 to 65, attributed his alcohol misuse to job stress and family difficulties; he had not consumed too much alcohol until 10–15 years ago and his excessive use persisted despite attempts to reduce it. He rejected abstinence and disulfiram and dropped out of earlier psychotherapy.

After a baseline period with a weekly mean of 3.4 binge drinking episodes (SD = 0.5), he received 12 one-hour sessions of metacognitive therapy and was followed up at 3 and 6 months. His metacognitive beliefs decreased gradually in the first half of treatment and then stayed stable, and he was classified as recovered with no DSM-5 AUD criteria met at post-treatment and follow-up.
